text: Lesson 29's custom rule just fired for real. This lesson picks up the exact incident it created and works it end to end — from the incident queue, through the investigation graph and an entity timeline, into a hunting query that checks for broader compromise, and out the other side with a bookmarked piece of evidence.

The incident lands in the queue as a Medium severity alert — impossible travel for one user account, carrying the Account entity and two IP address entities the rule mapped. It isn't a High, but two countries forty minutes apart earns a full look rather than a quick dismissal. Opening it is step one of every investigation in this course.

Inside the incident, the investigation graph renders the Account and both IP addresses as connected nodes. Expanding the Account node surfaces every other alert touching that same user automatically — exactly what the entity mapping work paid for. The entity timeline for that node lays out every sign-in and alert for this user in chronological order, showing where these two sign-ins actually sit.

One compromised account is bad; a hunting query checks whether it's the only one. Scoping SigninLogs to the incident's own two IP addresses and summarizing by UserPrincipalName and IPAddress answers the real follow-up question directly: did either address touch any other account in the last day, or does the scope stay contained to this one user?

Whatever that hunt returns, it's worth keeping past this session. A bookmark saves the query and its exact result set, tagged to this incident, so the next analyst — or the same analyst a week later — doesn't have to re-run it from memory. That's what turns a quick check into a documented part of the case file.

Queue, graph, timeline, hunt, bookmark — that's a complete investigation, and it's the same incident this lesson's case study follows next, from its very first raw log all the way through to how it actually gets closed.
